1	# TAC-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner
2	
3	Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
10	AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
11	*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?
12	
13	**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
14	Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
15	*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."
16	
17	**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
18	The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.
19	
20	**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
21	`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery
26	
27	**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
28	Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.
29	
30	**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
31	It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.
32	
33	**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
34	Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.
35	
36	**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
37	(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.
38	
39	**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
40	`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.
41	
42	**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
43	Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

# TAC-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?

**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."

**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.

**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.

**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.

**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.

**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.

**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.

**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.

**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.

**13. Pay to play.**
Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.

**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.

**15. The mission has named enemies.**
"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?

5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?

1	# TAC-8 · The Agentic Layer — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 63:19 · Advanced · Tactic #8: **Prioritize Agentics** — the final lesson and the compression of the whole course.
4	> Lesson artifact: five sibling codebases, each a working agentic layer at a different scale — from three near-empty directories (app1) to an agent living inside the product (app5).
5	> ⚠️ Capture note: the lesson video's screen content is live only to ~34:30; everything after (MCP demo payoff, the AEA demo, the recap, the final question) is audio-verified against the VTT, not frame-verified. Five lost beats are `diagram_instead` in the frame plan.
6	
7	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Your codebase now has two layers — the application layer and the agentic layer (deterministic ADW code fused with non-deterministic agentic prompts) — and the irreplaceable engineer spends most of their time thickening the second so it operates the first, guided daily by one question: *am I working on the agentic layer or the application layer?*
8	
9	**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Idea 1 — Tactic #8: Prioritize Agentics (the tactic that contains all tactics)
14	
15	**Hook.** Seven lessons, seven tactics — and the last one has "been staring us in the face the entire time." It isn't new machinery. It's an allocation decision you make every single day, and it decides whether you compound or plateau.
16	
17	**Picture.** No usable tactic-card frame exists (spoken over B-roll); render the reveal as a designed card. Support with frame t0385 (6:25) — the `ls` of five app directories — as the "here's where we practice it" shot.
18	
19	**Worked example.** The repo itself: five codebases where the application layer is deliberately boring (hello-world scripts, a tweets CSV, a demo SQL app) and every interesting file is agentic-layer. The lesson's time allocation mirrors the tactic's.
20	
21	**Dan's term.** *Prioritize agentics — prioritize your agentic layer.* The ratio: "at least half" of engineering time, more when bootstrapping. The compression claim: "This tactic represents all others, from target zero-touch engineering all the way back to stop coding."
22	
23	**Failure mode.** Agreeing in principle and then spending the week entirely in the application layer "because deadline." The tactic is behavioral, not attitudinal: if your calendar doesn't show agentic-layer hours, you don't practice it. (Dan's guardrail: deadlines are one of only three acceptable reasons — see Idea 9.)
24	
25	**Retrieval Q.** What is Tactic #8, what time split does it prescribe, and what does Dan say it compresses? *(Prioritize agentics; ≥50% on the agentic layer; all other tactics, ZTE back to stop coding.)*
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Idea 2 — The two layers and the ring
30	
31	**Hook.** Imagine a ring around your codebase. Thin at first. Every prompt you template, every workflow you script, thickens it — until machines that operate with your judgment are shipping your way, autonomously, in your product.
32	
33	**Picture.** The ring exists on screen only as a green pixel animation over B-roll (~1:10) — `diagram_instead`: draw the two-layer ring (application core; agentic ring of prompts/plans/ADWs; triggers piercing the ring from outside).
34	
35	**Worked example.** Every app in tac-8 enforces the split physically: `apps/` (or `app/`) is the application layer; `.claude/commands/` + `specs/` + `adws/` are the ring. app1's README states it as doctrine: "The Agentic Layer wraps your Application Layer, providing a programmatic interface for AI-driven development workflows."
36	
37	**Dan's term.** *The agentic layer* vs *the application layer* — and he's deliberately vague about the second: DevOps, infrastructure, database, raw app — "it all goes under there." The definition (~50:20, audio): "the combination of traditional deterministic code stored in your ADWs directory… with the new non-deterministic agentic technology… the old world of deterministic code and the new world of agentic prompts."
38	
39	**Failure mode.** Mixing layers: agent scripts inside the app, agents editing main without isolation. The separation isn't aesthetics — it's what lets the same ring shape wrap ANY application layer (Jupyter notebook in app2, Vue dashboard in app3, FastAPI product in app5), and what keeps the ring reusable while the app churns.
40	
41	**Retrieval Q.** Give Dan's two-ingredient definition of the agentic layer and name what lives under "application layer." *(Deterministic ADW code + non-deterministic agentic prompts/LM; DevOps, infra, database, raw application.)*
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Idea 3 — The Minimum Viable Agentic Layer (app1)
46	
47	**Hook.** What's the smallest agentic layer that's real? Three directories. Not a framework, not a platform — three directories and one rule.
48	
49	**Picture.** Frame t0430 (7:10): app1's README with the MVAL tree — `specs/` (plans), `.claude/commands/` (prompts), `adws/` (workflows) — each line commented. Frame t0515 (8:35): the in-loop warm-up, /prime running.
50	
51	**Worked example.** `tac8_app1__agent_layer_primitives`: five prompts (prime, start, chore, feature, implement), four ADW scripts over one core module, two hello-world app files. The one rule, verbatim: "The only thing that matters is that you can compose code and reference other files and have this be isolated from your application layer." Scripting language is explicitly free choice — UV Python (used all course), Bun TS, shell.
52	
53	**Dan's term.** *Minimum viable agentic layer.* Also the pieces' roles: prompts are the atoms ("none of this works without the prompts"); ADWs "combine the old world of deterministic guaranteed code execution with the new world of agents"; plans are what planning prompts emit and building prompts consume.
54	
55	**Failure mode.** Cargo-culting the scaled tree (hooks, triggers, state, worktrees, observability — app1's README shows it too) on day one. The lesson's growth model is thin-ring-first; the scaled tree is where you END after value compounds, not where you start.
56	
57	**Retrieval Q.** Name the MVAL's three pieces and the single scripting-layer rule. *(adws/ + .claude/commands/ + specs/; any language that composes code, references files, and stays isolated from the app layer.)*
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Idea 4 — The gateway script (adw_prompt.py) and the observability contract
62	
63	**Hook.** Somewhere in your codebase there's about to be a script that is categorically different from every other script you've ever written: it doesn't compute a result — it hires an intelligence and files a report about what happened.
64	
65	**Picture.** Frame t0810 (13:30): adw_prompt.py's UV header + the rich **Inputs** panel (ADW ID `d2c20425`, agent `oneoff`, prompt, model `sonnet`, working dir, output path) for Dan's live run: *"list all files in the adws directory and a concise output of their purpose."*
66	
67	**Worked example.** `adws/adw_prompt.py` → `adw_modules/agent.py`: builds `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format stream-json --model sonnet --dangerously-skip-permissions`, with retry logic and a filtered subprocess env. Everything lands under `agents/{adw_id}/{agent_name}/`: `cc_raw_output.jsonl` (stream) → `cc_raw_output.json` (array) → `cc_final_object.json` (final message) → `custom_summary_output.json` (your own metadata view). Dan: "this layer of control is really important."
68	
69	**Dan's term.** *The gateway into agentic coding.* "This ADW is calling an agent — this is distinctly different from any other type of code." Plus the forward pointer: the same call is available via the Claude Code SDK (Python/Bun) — app1 ships `agent_sdk.py` + `adw_sdk_prompt.py` — but TAC drives the CLI "to have full control over how the agent is called."
70	
71	**Failure mode.** Dismissing it as a wrapper and skipping the output tour. The four output files are the debugging/observability substrate every later system (task boards, Notion factory, AEA) assumes. If you can't say what's in `cc_final_object.json` vs the summary, the multi-agent lessons will feel like magic instead of engineering.
72	
73	**Retrieval Q.** What state does the gateway script manage around one agent call? *(Unique adw_id, retries, and agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/ outputs: JSONL stream, JSON array, final object, custom summary.)*
74	
75	---
76	
77	## Idea 5 — Template meta prompts: templating your engineering
78	
79	**Hook.** The most leveraged file in tac-8 isn't code. It's a markdown file that writes markdown files — your engineering standards compiled into a form compute can execute.
80	
81	**Picture.** Frame t0610 (10:10): chore.md open — Variables (adw_id, prompt), Instructions ("research the codebase starting with README.md"), and the **Plan Format** block. Frame t2065 (34:25): the specialized cousin, plan_uv_mcp.md, with its Workflow (`uv init --package --python 3.10`) and `ai_docs/mcp-python-sdk.md` reference.
82	
83	**Worked example.** The Plan Format is the load-bearing part: metadata, chore description, relevant files, **step-by-step tasks executed top to bottom**, and **validation commands** — the plan ends by checking itself (feedback loops, encoded). /implement is a *higher-order prompt*: it takes the plan as `$ARGUMENTS`. Specialization ladder: generic `/plan` → `/chore`, `/feature` → app4's `/plan_uv_mcp`, `/plan_vite_vue`, `/plan_uv_script`, `/plan_bun_scripts` ("You will be able to outperform these by going more specific").
84	
85	**Dan's term.** *Template meta prompts* — "prompts that output prompts in specific formats with specific rules, guidelines, files to read, conditional documentation." The design stance: "while you're building out your meta prompts, you want to be thinking from your agent's perspective — is this the engineering workflow you would use to solve the problem set at hand?" And the target: *problem classes, not one-off fixes.*
86	
87	**Failure mode.** Writing prompts so specific they solve today's task once. The class test: at ~38:50 one concise prompt produces an entire working MCP server, and Dan declares "I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV model context protocol servers. I've solved it. It's done." If your template can't absorb a request you didn't anticipate, you templated an instance, not a class.
88	
89	**Retrieval Q.** What makes a template meta prompt different from a good prompt, and what two sections make the Plan Format self-verifying? *(It generates another prompt (a plan) in a rigid format encoding your standards; step-by-step tasks + validation commands.)*
90	
91	---
92	
93	## Idea 6 — Composed ADWs: the chore→implement pipeline
94	
95	**Hook.** Two prompts and forty lines of glue: that's your first real AI developer workflow — and the glue is where the guarantees live.
96	
97	**Picture.** Frame t1131 (18:51): the money shot — **Planning Success** panel with the plan path, **Phase 2: Implementation** consuming that exact path as its argument, the generated spec (`chore-eae01d83-create-sh-version-main.md`) open in the editor, and `apps/main.sh` newly present in the tree.
98	
99	**Worked example.** `adws/adw_chore_implement.py`: Phase 1 `execute_template(/chore [adw_id, prompt])` as agent **planner** → `extract_plan_path()` regex-parses `specs/chore-*.md` from the agent's report (the /chore prompt's Report section is a CONTRACT: "Return the path to the plan file created") → Phase 2 `execute_template(/implement [plan_path])` as agent **builder** → per-phase summaries + `workflow_summary.json`. Dan's on-camera run: "create a .sh version of main in apps/*" — deliberately overkill ("we don't need this much compute for a simple task") to demonstrate *complete control* over the workflow.
100	
101	**Dan's term.** ADWs are "the highest abstraction level," the fusion of prompts with "the deterministic world of raw code," and "this begins infinite combinations and composables." He prefers the "nice explicit version" over clever chainable configs — "more readable, understandable for yourself, for your engineers, and most importantly for agents that you work with." Naming the pattern at scale (app2's variant): *an architect and an editor — ultra powerful pattern.*
102	
103	**Failure mode.** Missing that the pipeline works ONLY because the meta prompt's report format is machine-parseable. Change /chore's Report section and the regex breaks — the deterministic and non-deterministic halves are coupled by explicit contracts. (Also: the composed ADW that can't fail loudly — app1's version exits nonzero and aborts phase 2 if planning fails.)
104	
105	**Retrieval Q.** Trace the plan path through adw_chore_implement.py. *(/chore writes specs/chore-{adw_id}-{name}.md and reports the path per its Report contract; the script regex-extracts it; /implement receives it as its argument; both phases log under agents/{adw_id}/planner|builder.)*
106	
107	---
108	
109	## Idea 7 — Todone: a multi-agent system in a markdown file (app2)
110	
111	**Hook.** No queue, no database, no framework: a markdown file and a 5-second cron loop — and suddenly seven agents are doing data-science chores in parallel while Dan narrates, hands off: "I'm not doing this, by the way."
112	
113	**Picture.** Frame t1320 (22:00): tasks.md above the trigger's **Starting 7 Tasks** panel + "Creating Worktree". Frame t1400 (23:20): `[🟡, adw_id]` markers + one agent's Build Inputs panel. Frame t1540 (25:40): the full state vocabulary — ✅ with commit hashes, 🟡 in flight, ⏰ blocked. Frame t1720 (28:40): the sparse-checkout worktree opened as its own editor window.
114	
115	**Worked example.** The state machine (README + update_task.md): `[]` pending → `[🟡, adw_id]` → `[✅ commit_hash, adw_id]` | `[❌, adw_id] … // Failed: reason`; `[⏰]` eligible only when EVERY task above it in its worktree is ✅ (a ❌ above blocks forever). Tags are per-task config parsed from `{…}`: `{opus}` upgrades the model; `{adw_plan_implement_update_task}` upgrades the workflow (build-update → plan-implement-update). The trigger (`adw_trigger_cron_todone.py`, default 5s, max 5 concurrent) does a cheap regex pre-check, then delegates PARSING to an agent — `/process_tasks` returns eligible worktree groups as strict JSON. Worktrees: `/init_worktree` = `git worktree add --no-checkout trees/<name> -b <name>` + cone sparse-checkout of only the app2 directory + `.env` copy + empty initial commit — "double isolation."
116	
117	**Dan's term.** *Todone* (to-do → to-DONE), the *two-way task list* ("we're pushing past the overkilled chat-based UI"), *dedicated environments*, and the growth observation: your adws/ + prompts become "its own kind of micro codebase — a wrangle layer around your codebase," so engineer it properly and keep it out of apps/.
118	
119	**Failure mode.** Writing one giant task and never touching tags or ⏰ — you get a to-do list with extra steps instead of an orchestrator with dependencies, model routing, and workflow routing. Second failure: skipping the validation pass; Dan physically opens `trees/enhance-training-data`, greps `tweets_positive_only.csv` for `negative` (zero hits), and only then trusts the ✅.
120	
121	**Retrieval Q.** Full state machine of tasks.md including blocking, and what the two tags do. *(See above; {opus}=model, {adw_plan_implement_update_task}=workflow tier.)*
122	
123	---
124	
125	## Idea 8 — Out-loop factories: PITER on a Notion board (app4)
126	
127	**Hook.** The prompt input for your next application doesn't have to live in a terminal. Dan's lives in a Notion card — and a cron job builds the app while he's on his phone.
128	
129	**Picture.** Frame t1835 (30:35): the **Agentic Prototyper** board — four prototype tasks, one card open showing `workflow:plan prototype:vite_vue` + `execute`. Frame t2065 (34:25): the /plan_uv_mcp specialized template. (The board's five-column zoom-out and the MCP payoff are in the frozen-video region — design cards for them.)
130	
131	**Worked example.** `adw_trigger_cron_notion_tasks.py` polls every 15s (`--once` for testing — Dan uses it on camera): eligible = status *Not started* or *HIL Review* + trigger word `execute` (or `continue - <prompt>` for iteration); claims instantly (status→In progress + adw_id) to prevent double-pickup; `{{prototype: uv_script|vite_vue|bun_scripts|uv_mcp}}` routes to the matching specialized planner; `/make_worktree_name` (a one-purpose agent with a strict output contract: ONLY the name) → `/init_worktree` → plan → implement → `/update_notion_task` writes results + commit hash back. Agents spawn as `subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True)` — detached, parallel, monitor-restart-proof. Payoff (audio region): the system-info MCP server — `.mcp.json` wired, `get_memory_info`/`get_cpu`/`get_disk` called live from Claude Code — from ONE concise prompt.
132	
133	**Dan's term.** *PITER, applied*: "Prompt input — for us, it's this Notion page. Environment — the trees directory… And then we have the review system" (the board's Not started / In progress / **Human in the loop review** / Failed / Done columns + live status updates). Plus the velocity claim: "Look at our velocity. Our velocity is absolutely mind-blowing."
134	
135	**Failure mode.** Assuming the review column is bureaucracy. HIL Review + `continue - <prompt>` is the iteration loop — the mechanism that lets you steer a factory without entering the loop. Skip it and your out-loop system is fire-and-forget, which is fire-and-regret at scale. Second failure: vague prototype cards ("build me a website") — the README's own anti-patterns.
136	
137	**Retrieval Q.** Map PITER onto app4 and name the claim mechanism that prevents duplicate work. *(Prompt input=Notion card; Trigger=15s cron; Environment=trees/ worktrees; Review=board columns+updates. Instant status flip to In progress with adw_id.)*
138	
139	---

141	## Idea 9 — One agent, one prompt, one purpose — and the AEA exception (app5)
142	
143	**Hook.** The most controversial rule in TAC ends with a confession: Dan breaks it exactly once, on purpose, inside his own product — to put an agent IN the app.
144	
145	**Picture.** Both AEA frames are lost to the capture freeze — design a mock: the NLQ-to-SQL app with two chat windows ("Nexus", "Roon"), the Cmd+P dev console (`/aea`, `/list`, `/toggle-view`, `/close-all`), annotated with the flow client → AEA server (port 8743) → SQLite (agent_id, cc_session_id, conversation) → `adw_aea_patch.py` → `claude -p … --resume <cc_session_id>`.
146	
147	**Worked example.** Every other agent in the whole course is one Claude instance, one prompt, one purpose — "focused agents, focused context windows, that are reproducible and easily testable, validatable, and improvable." app5's AEA server is the sanctioned exception: it persists `cc_session_id` and passes it back with `--resume`, because a conversational product agent NEEDS continuity across prompts, refreshes, and server restarts. The demo (audio region): `/aea` → Nexus answers "what is this codebase about?" while a second agent Roon renames the Generate-Random-Query button — parallel, in-product. "The power of agents isn't in one, it's in many."
148	
149	**Dan's term.** *One agent, one prompt, one purpose*; *AEA — agent embedded application*; and the reframe: "we have a dedicated agent-embedded application server so that we can access this outside the loop. In this case, outside the loop is inside the application." Rule-breaking is explicit: "We broke one of our rules."
150	
151	**Failure mode.** Two symmetric ones: treating the rule as optional (sprawling multi-topic mega-agents whose context windows can't be reproduced or tested) — or treating it as absolute (refusing session continuity even where the use case demands it). The lesson models the discipline: break the rule once, knowingly, with the mechanism (DB-persisted session id) engineered for it.
152	
153	**Retrieval Q.** State the rule, why it exists, and the single exception with its mechanism. *(Focused/reproducible/testable context windows; app5 AEA resumes conversations via stored cc_session_id + --resume.)*
154	
155	---

157	## Idea 10 — The compression: KPIs → PITE → one question
158	
159	**Hook.** The course ends by deleting itself: eight tactics, twelve leverage points, four KPIs — compressed into one question you ask every day, and one letter you eventually drop.
160	
161	**Picture.** All in the frozen-video region — design three cards: the KPI quad (attempts ↓, size ↑, streak ↑, presence → 0); PITER→PITE with the R crossed out and replaced by encoded feedback loops; and the full-bleed final question.
162	
163	**Worked example.** The recap runs the whole stack against the codebases you just used: feedback loops = the validation commands in every Plan Format ("There is a validation, a set of validations in your codebase that once run ensures everything works perfectly — the only question is, do you know what it is?"); ZTE = ship a dialed-in ADW until "the time you spend reviewing the work will be useless… you realize you're the bottleneck," then PITER→PITE. The final question (~52:39): **"Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer?"** — with exactly three acceptable reasons to answer "application": a deadline, testing something, or running prompts in-loop to verify they'll work out-loop. Anything else is "moving sideways while other engineers move up." Closing frame of the whole course: "When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence."
164	
165	**Dan's term.** *The final question / final meta tactic*, teased at ~2:14 as "the oil of this course." Plus the economic stakes: *the commoditization of implementation* ("with agentic coding, not only is code a commodity, but the implementation as well"), value moving up the stack (system design, domain encoding, quality control, creative problem decomposition — "which you'll then encode in your ADWs"), and the identity: "An agentic engineer operates on living pieces of software that work while they sleep."
166	
167	**Failure mode.** Answering the question once, at course end, instead of daily at sit-down. And the ego failure Dan names twice: believing you can outperform "your team's best engineering practices encoded into a template metaprompt that runs in an ADW that kicks off five to ten agents per problem… don't try to compete with that — your place of competition is now net new innovation."
168	
169	**Retrieval Q.** The final question, the three exemptions, and the PITE prerequisite. *(See above; drop the R only after feedback loops + reliability streaks prove review is the bottleneck.)*

# TAC-8 · The Agentic Layer — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 63:19 · Advanced · Tactic #8: **Prioritize Agentics** — the final lesson and the compression of the whole course.
> Lesson artifact: five sibling codebases, each a working agentic layer at a different scale — from three near-empty directories (app1) to an agent living inside the product (app5).
> ⚠️ Capture note: the lesson video's screen content is live only to ~34:30; everything after (MCP demo payoff, the AEA demo, the recap, the final question) is audio-verified against the VTT, not frame-verified. Five lost beats are `diagram_instead` in the frame plan.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Your codebase now has two layers — the application layer and the agentic layer (deterministic ADW code fused with non-deterministic agentic prompts) — and the irreplaceable engineer spends most of their time thickening the second so it operates the first, guided daily by one question: *am I working on the agentic layer or the application layer?*

**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — Tactic #8: Prioritize Agentics (the tactic that contains all tactics)

**Hook.** Seven lessons, seven tactics — and the last one has "been staring us in the face the entire time." It isn't new machinery. It's an allocation decision you make every single day, and it decides whether you compound or plateau.

**Picture.** No usable tactic-card frame exists (spoken over B-roll); render the reveal as a designed card. Support with frame t0385 (6:25) — the `ls` of five app directories — as the "here's where we practice it" shot.

**Worked example.** The repo itself: five codebases where the application layer is deliberately boring (hello-world scripts, a tweets CSV, a demo SQL app) and every interesting file is agentic-layer. The lesson's time allocation mirrors the tactic's.

**Dan's term.** *Prioritize agentics — prioritize your agentic layer.* The ratio: "at least half" of engineering time, more when bootstrapping. The compression claim: "This tactic represents all others, from target zero-touch engineering all the way back to stop coding."

**Failure mode.** Agreeing in principle and then spending the week entirely in the application layer "because deadline." The tactic is behavioral, not attitudinal: if your calendar doesn't show agentic-layer hours, you don't practice it. (Dan's guardrail: deadlines are one of only three acceptable reasons — see Idea 9.)

**Retrieval Q.** What is Tactic #8, what time split does it prescribe, and what does Dan say it compresses? *(Prioritize agentics; ≥50% on the agentic layer; all other tactics, ZTE back to stop coding.)*

---

## Idea 2 — The two layers and the ring

**Hook.** Imagine a ring around your codebase. Thin at first. Every prompt you template, every workflow you script, thickens it — until machines that operate with your judgment are shipping your way, autonomously, in your product.

**Picture.** The ring exists on screen only as a green pixel animation over B-roll (~1:10) — `diagram_instead`: draw the two-layer ring (application core; agentic ring of prompts/plans/ADWs; triggers piercing the ring from outside).

**Worked example.** Every app in tac-8 enforces the split physically: `apps/` (or `app/`) is the application layer; `.claude/commands/` + `specs/` + `adws/` are the ring. app1's README states it as doctrine: "The Agentic Layer wraps your Application Layer, providing a programmatic interface for AI-driven development workflows."

**Dan's term.** *The agentic layer* vs *the application layer* — and he's deliberately vague about the second: DevOps, infrastructure, database, raw app — "it all goes under there." The definition (~50:20, audio): "the combination of traditional deterministic code stored in your ADWs directory… with the new non-deterministic agentic technology… the old world of deterministic code and the new world of agentic prompts."

**Failure mode.** Mixing layers: agent scripts inside the app, agents editing main without isolation. The separation isn't aesthetics — it's what lets the same ring shape wrap ANY application layer (Jupyter notebook in app2, Vue dashboard in app3, FastAPI product in app5), and what keeps the ring reusable while the app churns.

**Retrieval Q.** Give Dan's two-ingredient definition of the agentic layer and name what lives under "application layer." *(Deterministic ADW code + non-deterministic agentic prompts/LM; DevOps, infra, database, raw application.)*

---

## Idea 3 — The Minimum Viable Agentic Layer (app1)

**Hook.** What's the smallest agentic layer that's real? Three directories. Not a framework, not a platform — three directories and one rule.

**Picture.** Frame t0430 (7:10): app1's README with the MVAL tree — `specs/` (plans), `.claude/commands/` (prompts), `adws/` (workflows) — each line commented. Frame t0515 (8:35): the in-loop warm-up, /prime running.

**Worked example.** `tac8_app1__agent_layer_primitives`: five prompts (prime, start, chore, feature, implement), four ADW scripts over one core module, two hello-world app files. The one rule, verbatim: "The only thing that matters is that you can compose code and reference other files and have this be isolated from your application layer." Scripting language is explicitly free choice — UV Python (used all course), Bun TS, shell.

**Dan's term.** *Minimum viable agentic layer.* Also the pieces' roles: prompts are the atoms ("none of this works without the prompts"); ADWs "combine the old world of deterministic guaranteed code execution with the new world of agents"; plans are what planning prompts emit and building prompts consume.

**Failure mode.** Cargo-culting the scaled tree (hooks, triggers, state, worktrees, observability — app1's README shows it too) on day one. The lesson's growth model is thin-ring-first; the scaled tree is where you END after value compounds, not where you start.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the MVAL's three pieces and the single scripting-layer rule. *(adws/ + .claude/commands/ + specs/; any language that composes code, references files, and stays isolated from the app layer.)*

---

## Idea 4 — The gateway script (adw_prompt.py) and the observability contract

**Hook.** Somewhere in your codebase there's about to be a script that is categorically different from every other script you've ever written: it doesn't compute a result — it hires an intelligence and files a report about what happened.

**Picture.** Frame t0810 (13:30): adw_prompt.py's UV header + the rich **Inputs** panel (ADW ID `d2c20425`, agent `oneoff`, prompt, model `sonnet`, working dir, output path) for Dan's live run: *"list all files in the adws directory and a concise output of their purpose."*

**Worked example.** `adws/adw_prompt.py` → `adw_modules/agent.py`: builds `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format stream-json --model sonnet --dangerously-skip-permissions`, with retry logic and a filtered subprocess env. Everything lands under `agents/{adw_id}/{agent_name}/`: `cc_raw_output.jsonl` (stream) → `cc_raw_output.json` (array) → `cc_final_object.json` (final message) → `custom_summary_output.json` (your own metadata view). Dan: "this layer of control is really important."

**Dan's term.** *The gateway into agentic coding.* "This ADW is calling an agent — this is distinctly different from any other type of code." Plus the forward pointer: the same call is available via the Claude Code SDK (Python/Bun) — app1 ships `agent_sdk.py` + `adw_sdk_prompt.py` — but TAC drives the CLI "to have full control over how the agent is called."

**Failure mode.** Dismissing it as a wrapper and skipping the output tour. The four output files are the debugging/observability substrate every later system (task boards, Notion factory, AEA) assumes. If you can't say what's in `cc_final_object.json` vs the summary, the multi-agent lessons will feel like magic instead of engineering.

**Retrieval Q.** What state does the gateway script manage around one agent call? *(Unique adw_id, retries, and agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/ outputs: JSONL stream, JSON array, final object, custom summary.)*

---

## Idea 5 — Template meta prompts: templating your engineering

**Hook.** The most leveraged file in tac-8 isn't code. It's a markdown file that writes markdown files — your engineering standards compiled into a form compute can execute.

**Picture.** Frame t0610 (10:10): chore.md open — Variables (adw_id, prompt), Instructions ("research the codebase starting with README.md"), and the **Plan Format** block. Frame t2065 (34:25): the specialized cousin, plan_uv_mcp.md, with its Workflow (`uv init --package --python 3.10`) and `ai_docs/mcp-python-sdk.md` reference.

**Worked example.** The Plan Format is the load-bearing part: metadata, chore description, relevant files, **step-by-step tasks executed top to bottom**, and **validation commands** — the plan ends by checking itself (feedback loops, encoded). /implement is a *higher-order prompt*: it takes the plan as `$ARGUMENTS`. Specialization ladder: generic `/plan` → `/chore`, `/feature` → app4's `/plan_uv_mcp`, `/plan_vite_vue`, `/plan_uv_script`, `/plan_bun_scripts` ("You will be able to outperform these by going more specific").

**Dan's term.** *Template meta prompts* — "prompts that output prompts in specific formats with specific rules, guidelines, files to read, conditional documentation." The design stance: "while you're building out your meta prompts, you want to be thinking from your agent's perspective — is this the engineering workflow you would use to solve the problem set at hand?" And the target: *problem classes, not one-off fixes.*

**Failure mode.** Writing prompts so specific they solve today's task once. The class test: at ~38:50 one concise prompt produces an entire working MCP server, and Dan declares "I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV model context protocol servers. I've solved it. It's done." If your template can't absorb a request you didn't anticipate, you templated an instance, not a class.

**Retrieval Q.** What makes a template meta prompt different from a good prompt, and what two sections make the Plan Format self-verifying? *(It generates another prompt (a plan) in a rigid format encoding your standards; step-by-step tasks + validation commands.)*

---

## Idea 6 — Composed ADWs: the chore→implement pipeline

**Hook.** Two prompts and forty lines of glue: that's your first real AI developer workflow — and the glue is where the guarantees live.

**Picture.** Frame t1131 (18:51): the money shot — **Planning Success** panel with the plan path, **Phase 2: Implementation** consuming that exact path as its argument, the generated spec (`chore-eae01d83-create-sh-version-main.md`) open in the editor, and `apps/main.sh` newly present in the tree.

**Worked example.** `adws/adw_chore_implement.py`: Phase 1 `execute_template(/chore [adw_id, prompt])` as agent **planner** → `extract_plan_path()` regex-parses `specs/chore-*.md` from the agent's report (the /chore prompt's Report section is a CONTRACT: "Return the path to the plan file created") → Phase 2 `execute_template(/implement [plan_path])` as agent **builder** → per-phase summaries + `workflow_summary.json`. Dan's on-camera run: "create a .sh version of main in apps/*" — deliberately overkill ("we don't need this much compute for a simple task") to demonstrate *complete control* over the workflow.

**Dan's term.** ADWs are "the highest abstraction level," the fusion of prompts with "the deterministic world of raw code," and "this begins infinite combinations and composables." He prefers the "nice explicit version" over clever chainable configs — "more readable, understandable for yourself, for your engineers, and most importantly for agents that you work with." Naming the pattern at scale (app2's variant): *an architect and an editor — ultra powerful pattern.*

**Failure mode.** Missing that the pipeline works ONLY because the meta prompt's report format is machine-parseable. Change /chore's Report section and the regex breaks — the deterministic and non-deterministic halves are coupled by explicit contracts. (Also: the composed ADW that can't fail loudly — app1's version exits nonzero and aborts phase 2 if planning fails.)

**Retrieval Q.** Trace the plan path through adw_chore_implement.py. *(/chore writes specs/chore-{adw_id}-{name}.md and reports the path per its Report contract; the script regex-extracts it; /implement receives it as its argument; both phases log under agents/{adw_id}/planner|builder.)*

---

## Idea 7 — Todone: a multi-agent system in a markdown file (app2)

**Hook.** No queue, no database, no framework: a markdown file and a 5-second cron loop — and suddenly seven agents are doing data-science chores in parallel while Dan narrates, hands off: "I'm not doing this, by the way."

**Picture.** Frame t1320 (22:00): tasks.md above the trigger's **Starting 7 Tasks** panel + "Creating Worktree". Frame t1400 (23:20): `[🟡, adw_id]` markers + one agent's Build Inputs panel. Frame t1540 (25:40): the full state vocabulary — ✅ with commit hashes, 🟡 in flight, ⏰ blocked. Frame t1720 (28:40): the sparse-checkout worktree opened as its own editor window.

**Worked example.** The state machine (README + update_task.md): `[]` pending → `[🟡, adw_id]` → `[✅ commit_hash, adw_id]` | `[❌, adw_id] … // Failed: reason`; `[⏰]` eligible only when EVERY task above it in its worktree is ✅ (a ❌ above blocks forever). Tags are per-task config parsed from `{…}`: `{opus}` upgrades the model; `{adw_plan_implement_update_task}` upgrades the workflow (build-update → plan-implement-update). The trigger (`adw_trigger_cron_todone.py`, default 5s, max 5 concurrent) does a cheap regex pre-check, then delegates PARSING to an agent — `/process_tasks` returns eligible worktree groups as strict JSON. Worktrees: `/init_worktree` = `git worktree add --no-checkout trees/<name> -b <name>` + cone sparse-checkout of only the app2 directory + `.env` copy + empty initial commit — "double isolation."

**Dan's term.** *Todone* (to-do → to-DONE), the *two-way task list* ("we're pushing past the overkilled chat-based UI"), *dedicated environments*, and the growth observation: your adws/ + prompts become "its own kind of micro codebase — a wrangle layer around your codebase," so engineer it properly and keep it out of apps/.

**Failure mode.** Writing one giant task and never touching tags or ⏰ — you get a to-do list with extra steps instead of an orchestrator with dependencies, model routing, and workflow routing. Second failure: skipping the validation pass; Dan physically opens `trees/enhance-training-data`, greps `tweets_positive_only.csv` for `negative` (zero hits), and only then trusts the ✅.

**Retrieval Q.** Full state machine of tasks.md including blocking, and what the two tags do. *(See above; {opus}=model, {adw_plan_implement_update_task}=workflow tier.)*

---

## Idea 8 — Out-loop factories: PITER on a Notion board (app4)

**Hook.** The prompt input for your next application doesn't have to live in a terminal. Dan's lives in a Notion card — and a cron job builds the app while he's on his phone.

**Picture.** Frame t1835 (30:35): the **Agentic Prototyper** board — four prototype tasks, one card open showing `workflow:plan prototype:vite_vue` + `execute`. Frame t2065 (34:25): the /plan_uv_mcp specialized template. (The board's five-column zoom-out and the MCP payoff are in the frozen-video region — design cards for them.)

**Worked example.** `adw_trigger_cron_notion_tasks.py` polls every 15s (`--once` for testing — Dan uses it on camera): eligible = status *Not started* or *HIL Review* + trigger word `execute` (or `continue - <prompt>` for iteration); claims instantly (status→In progress + adw_id) to prevent double-pickup; `{{prototype: uv_script|vite_vue|bun_scripts|uv_mcp}}` routes to the matching specialized planner; `/make_worktree_name` (a one-purpose agent with a strict output contract: ONLY the name) → `/init_worktree` → plan → implement → `/update_notion_task` writes results + commit hash back. Agents spawn as `subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True)` — detached, parallel, monitor-restart-proof. Payoff (audio region): the system-info MCP server — `.mcp.json` wired, `get_memory_info`/`get_cpu`/`get_disk` called live from Claude Code — from ONE concise prompt.

**Dan's term.** *PITER, applied*: "Prompt input — for us, it's this Notion page. Environment — the trees directory… And then we have the review system" (the board's Not started / In progress / **Human in the loop review** / Failed / Done columns + live status updates). Plus the velocity claim: "Look at our velocity. Our velocity is absolutely mind-blowing."

**Failure mode.** Assuming the review column is bureaucracy. HIL Review + `continue - <prompt>` is the iteration loop — the mechanism that lets you steer a factory without entering the loop. Skip it and your out-loop system is fire-and-forget, which is fire-and-regret at scale. Second failure: vague prototype cards ("build me a website") — the README's own anti-patterns.

**Retrieval Q.** Map PITER onto app4 and name the claim mechanism that prevents duplicate work. *(Prompt input=Notion card; Trigger=15s cron; Environment=trees/ worktrees; Review=board columns+updates. Instant status flip to In progress with adw_id.)*

---

## Idea 9 — One agent, one prompt, one purpose — and the AEA exception (app5)

**Hook.** The most controversial rule in TAC ends with a confession: Dan breaks it exactly once, on purpose, inside his own product — to put an agent IN the app.

**Picture.** Both AEA frames are lost to the capture freeze — design a mock: the NLQ-to-SQL app with two chat windows ("Nexus", "Roon"), the Cmd+P dev console (`/aea`, `/list`, `/toggle-view`, `/close-all`), annotated with the flow client → AEA server (port 8743) → SQLite (agent_id, cc_session_id, conversation) → `adw_aea_patch.py` → `claude -p … --resume <cc_session_id>`.

**Worked example.** Every other agent in the whole course is one Claude instance, one prompt, one purpose — "focused agents, focused context windows, that are reproducible and easily testable, validatable, and improvable." app5's AEA server is the sanctioned exception: it persists `cc_session_id` and passes it back with `--resume`, because a conversational product agent NEEDS continuity across prompts, refreshes, and server restarts. The demo (audio region): `/aea` → Nexus answers "what is this codebase about?" while a second agent Roon renames the Generate-Random-Query button — parallel, in-product. "The power of agents isn't in one, it's in many."

**Dan's term.** *One agent, one prompt, one purpose*; *AEA — agent embedded application*; and the reframe: "we have a dedicated agent-embedded application server so that we can access this outside the loop. In this case, outside the loop is inside the application." Rule-breaking is explicit: "We broke one of our rules."

**Failure mode.** Two symmetric ones: treating the rule as optional (sprawling multi-topic mega-agents whose context windows can't be reproduced or tested) — or treating it as absolute (refusing session continuity even where the use case demands it). The lesson models the discipline: break the rule once, knowingly, with the mechanism (DB-persisted session id) engineered for it.

**Retrieval Q.** State the rule, why it exists, and the single exception with its mechanism. *(Focused/reproducible/testable context windows; app5 AEA resumes conversations via stored cc_session_id + --resume.)*

---

## Idea 10 — The compression: KPIs → PITE → one question

**Hook.** The course ends by deleting itself: eight tactics, twelve leverage points, four KPIs — compressed into one question you ask every day, and one letter you eventually drop.

**Picture.** All in the frozen-video region — design three cards: the KPI quad (attempts ↓, size ↑, streak ↑, presence → 0); PITER→PITE with the R crossed out and replaced by encoded feedback loops; and the full-bleed final question.

**Worked example.** The recap runs the whole stack against the codebases you just used: feedback loops = the validation commands in every Plan Format ("There is a validation, a set of validations in your codebase that once run ensures everything works perfectly — the only question is, do you know what it is?"); ZTE = ship a dialed-in ADW until "the time you spend reviewing the work will be useless… you realize you're the bottleneck," then PITER→PITE. The final question (~52:39): **"Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer?"** — with exactly three acceptable reasons to answer "application": a deadline, testing something, or running prompts in-loop to verify they'll work out-loop. Anything else is "moving sideways while other engineers move up." Closing frame of the whole course: "When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence."

**Dan's term.** *The final question / final meta tactic*, teased at ~2:14 as "the oil of this course." Plus the economic stakes: *the commoditization of implementation* ("with agentic coding, not only is code a commodity, but the implementation as well"), value moving up the stack (system design, domain encoding, quality control, creative problem decomposition — "which you'll then encode in your ADWs"), and the identity: "An agentic engineer operates on living pieces of software that work while they sleep."

**Failure mode.** Answering the question once, at course end, instead of daily at sit-down. And the ego failure Dan names twice: believing you can outperform "your team's best engineering practices encoded into a template metaprompt that runs in an ADW that kicks off five to ten agents per problem… don't try to compete with that — your place of competition is now net new innovation."

**Retrieval Q.** The final question, the three exemptions, and the PITE prerequisite. *(See above; drop the R only after feedback loops + reliability streaks prove review is the bottleneck.)*

## Terminology glossary (Dan-isms, canonical spellings)

- **The agentic layer** — deterministic ADW code + non-deterministic agentic prompts, wrapped as a ring around the application layer
- **The application layer** — everything classical: app, database, infra, DevOps
- **MVAL (minimum viable agentic layer)** — adws/ + .claude/commands/ + specs/
- **Template meta prompt** — a prompt that generates a prompt (a plan) in a rigid format; *plan format* is its load-bearing section
- **Higher-order prompt** — a prompt that takes another prompt/plan as an argument (/implement)
- **The gateway script** — adw_prompt.py; the smallest ADW: one prompt, managed state
- **ADW** — AI Developer Workflow; "the highest level of composition — code plus agentics"
- **Todone** — app2's to-do→to-DONE multi-agent task system; tasks.md is a *two-way task list*
- **Trigger** — the mechanism that fires ADWs without you (cron over tasks.md, Notion poller, webhook, AEA server)
- **PITER / PITE** — Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review — until you drop the R (ZTE)

- **AEA** — Agent Embedded Application (app5); agents living inside the product

- **Agentic KPIs** — attempts ↓, size ↑, streak ↑, presence → 0

input.content:
# TAC-8 Lab Spec — The Agentic Layer

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-8`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-8.git`). Five sibling apps live inside it; you touch four (app3 is skipped on camera and here). No external repos.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Agents write `main.sh`, the enhanced datasets, the prototypes, and the MCP server. You write only prompts, plans, tasks, and ADW glue. Even edits go through Claude Code.
**The one question (asked at every checkpoint):** *am I working on the agentic layer or in the application layer?* This lab is 100% agentic-layer work by construction — that is the point.
**Time box:** core reproduction 90–150 min; with stretch drills 3–5 hours. Token cost: real and non-trivial — app2 alone kicks off ~7 agents, app4 spawns detached prototypers. Pay to play; budget API funds or a plan before you start.
**Safety note (do not skip):** every tac-8 ADW runs Claude with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Stay inside the cloned repo, and **read each prompt/ADW file before you fire it**. This is a graded habit, not a formality.

---

## 0 · Setup (15 min)

1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-8.git && cd tac-8` (catalog mirror: `tac/tac-8`).
2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `bun --version`, `git --version`. Windows: run everything inside WSL. Confirm `git worktree` works (`git worktree list`).
3. In `tac8_app1__agent_layer_primitives`: `cp .env.sample .env` and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (plus `CLAUDE_CODE_PATH` if `claude` isn't on your PATH).
4. **Read app1's `README.md` end to end.** Before running anything, answer in writing:
   - Name the **three MVAL pieces** and the **two layers**.
   - Which directory is the application layer here, and which directories form the ring?

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, the two layers and the MVAL's three pieces (`adws/` + `.claude/commands/` + `specs/`). If you can't, re-read the README — this vocabulary carries the whole lesson.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — app1, the primitives (30–40 min)

**A. In-loop warm-up.** Run `claude`, then `/prime`. Confirm it runs `git ls-files`, reads both READMEs, and reports. Then `/start`; confirm both hello-world outputs. *(This is the "set your agent up" baseline before any out-loop machinery.)*

**B. The gateway script.** `./adws/adw_prompt.py "list all files in the adws directory and a concise output of their purpose"` — Dan's exact run. Read the **Inputs** panel (ADW ID, agent `oneoff`, prompt, model, working dir, output path), then inspect all four files under `agents/<adw_id>/oneoff/`.

**Checkpoint 1B (write it down):** in one line each, what does `cc_raw_output.jsonl` vs `cc_raw_output.json` vs `cc_final_object.json` vs `custom_summary_output.json` contain? This observability tree is assumed by every later system.

**C. Slash, out of the loop.** `./adws/adw_slash_command.py /start` — same behavior as the in-loop `/start`, zero conversation. Note: you just ran a prompt with no chat window. That is "moving out the loop" in one command.

**D. Composed ADW (Dan's exact run).** `./adws/adw_chore_implement.py "create a .sh version of main in apps/*"`. Verify: `specs/chore-<id>-*.md` exists; `apps/main.sh` exists and runs (`sh apps/main.sh`); `agents/<adw_id>/` contains `planner/` + `builder/` + `workflow_summary.json`.

**Checkpoint 1D:** trace the plan path in one sentence — `/chore` writes `specs/chore-{id}-*.md` and *reports the path per its Report contract*; the script regex-extracts it; `/implement` receives it as its argument. Say why editing `/chore`'s Report section would break the pipeline. *(The deterministic script and the non-deterministic prompt are coupled by an explicit machine-parseable contract.)*

## 2 · Reproduce Dan — app2 Todone, multi-agent (30–45 min)

1. **Author a board.** Replace `tasks.md` content with your own `# ATL` list: two worktrees, three tasks each; mark the last task of one worktree `[⏰]`; tag one task `{opus}` and one `{sonnet, adw_plan_implement_update_task}`.
2. **Trigger once (dry first).** `./adws/adw_triggers/adw_trigger_cron_todone.py --once --dry-run` (read what WOULD happen), then `--once` for real. Watch worktree creation and `🟡` markers appear in `tasks.md`.
3. **Let it drain.** Run the trigger with defaults (5s poll). Verify `✅` lines carry real commit hashes (`git -C trees/<name> log --oneline`) and that the `⏰` task started **only after** everything above it in its worktree succeeded.
4. **Validation pass (Dan's move).** `code trees/<worktree>` — confirm the sparse checkout contains **only** `tac8_app2__multi_agent_todone`. Validate one agent's artifact by hand exactly like Dan validated `tweets_positive_only.csv` (open it, grep for what must NOT be there, confirm zero hits) — only then trust the `✅`.

**Checkpoint 2:** recite the tasks.md state machine — `[]` → `[🟡, adw_id]` → `[✅ commit_hash, adw_id]` | `[❌, adw_id] // Failed: reason`; `[⏰]` eligible only when every task above it is `✅` — and say what each tag does (`{opus}` = model tier, `{adw_plan_implement_update_task}` = workflow tier).

## 3 · Reproduce Dan — app4 prototyping, no Notion required (15–25 min)

1. Read `adw_trigger_cron_notion_tasks.py`'s **claim → route → spawn** flow and `.claude/commands/plan_uv_mcp.md`.
2. Run the specialized meta prompt in-loop: `claude` → `/plan_uv_mcp test0001 "Create a concise and minimal MCP server that provides system information: memory, cpu, disk"`. Read the generated `specs/plan-*-uv-mcp.md` and check it against the **Plan Format** contract (metadata, chore description, relevant files, step-by-step tasks, **validation commands**).
3. Confirm the routing table maps `{{prototype: uv_mcp}}` → `/plan_uv_mcp` and `continue - <prompt>` → HIL iteration (README §How It Works).

**Checkpoint 3:** map PITER onto app4 out loud — Prompt input = Notion card; Trigger = 15s cron; Environment = `trees/` worktrees; Review = board columns + live status. Name the mechanism that prevents two triggers grabbing the same card. *(Instant status flip to In progress + adw_id on claim.)*

## 4 · Reproduce Dan — app5 AEA, agents in the product (15–25 min)

1. `cp app/server/.env.sample app/server/.env` (add keys); `./scripts/start.sh`; in a second terminal `./scripts/aea_server_start.sh` (edit `CLAUDE_CODE_PATH` for your machine).

# TAC-8 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

TAC-8 ages well for the same reason TAC-1 does: it teaches an allocation decision and a set of primitives, not a toolchain. Dan future-proofs it on camera — *"keep your eyes on the primitives… Claude Code represents the first viable engineering tool that unlocks agentic engineering, but it won't be the last."* The **concepts** (two layers, MVAL, template meta prompts, ADWs, triggers, PITER→PITE, the guiding question) are unchanged. What has moved is the **packaging** of each primitive — every hand-rolled mechanism in the five apps now has a first-class successor. Seven gaps; for each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.

---

## 1. Reusable behavior: `.claude/commands/*.md` libraries → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap

**Course era:** every reusable behavior is a slash-command prompt file (`.claude/commands/chore.md`, `plan_uv_mcp.md`, `process_tasks.md`…) invoked by name from ADWs. This is "template your engineering" done primitively — and pedagogically perfect, because there's no magic to hide behind.
**Current:** Claude Code packages reusable expertise as **Agent Skills** — `SKILL.md` with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand, shareable across repos and teams. The lesson's meta-prompt concept maps 1:1; discovery, triggering, and composition all upgraded.
**Book treatment:** overlay + sidebar. Teach the `.claude/commands` form first (it's the load-bearing concept), then show the same template as a Skill.
**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (already anchors the TAC-1 chapter; **defer** here to avoid double-placement — see table).

## 2. The agent call: hand-rolled subprocess `agent.py` → Claude Agent SDK

**Course era:** every app copies a ~630-line `agent.py` that shells out to `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format stream-json --model <m> --dangerously-skip-permissions`, with retry logic, a filtered subprocess env, and hand-parsed JSONL landing under `agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/`. Dan drives the CLI deliberately, "to have full control over how the agent is called."
**Current:** Dan already plants the successor on camera — app1 ships `agent_sdk.py` + `adw_sdk_prompt.py`, "a Python version and a bun version." That matured into the **Claude Agent SDK** (Python/TS): typed messages, sessions, hooks, subagents, structured outputs. Production ADWs start there; the subprocess form remains the clearest *teaching* form.
**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the ~630-line wrapper you're reading has a supported grown-up form"), not a rewrite — the concept (agent as a callable, observable component) is unchanged.
**Overlay:** none needed.

## 3. Permissions: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` everywhere → modes, sandboxing, hooks

**Course era:** all tac-8 ADWs bypass permissions entirely — fine for isolated throwaway demo repos, dangerous as a default habit.
**Current:** headless agents are gated with allowlists, **permission modes** (plan/accept-edits/…), sandboxed bash, deny rules, and pre/post tool-use **hooks**. The lesson's *isolation* instinct — git worktrees + sparse checkout, "double isolation" — is exactly right and is now complemented by first-class sandboxing; the blanket bypass flag is the dated part.
**Book treatment:** "current practice" callout on every `--dangerously-skip-permissions` screenshot. Teach the isolation habit as timeless; flag the flag.
**Overlay:** none needed.

**Course era:** app2/app4 poll with `schedule` loops inside long-running terminal processes (5s / 15s); app5 hand-rolls a FastAPI server. The trigger CONCEPT — the mechanism that fires ADWs without you — is the durable idea.

**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. Keep the hand-rolled poller as the transparent teaching version; point to managed triggers as the production target.
**Overlay:** none needed (the trigger primitive is covered in-lesson).

**Course era:** parallelism is achieved at the OS level — detached `subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True)` per task, one Claude instance each, coordinated by markdown (`tasks.md`) or Notion state. Impressive, and deliberately transparent.
**Current:** in-band multi-agent primitives — subagents, parallel tool fan-out, worktree-isolated background agents, orchestration frameworks — express the same patterns inside the agent runtime, with less scaffolding. Same architecture, less glue.
**Book treatment:** forward-pointer + "current practice" note. The lesson's OS-level version is the best way to *understand* the architecture; note that the runtime now offers it natively.

**Current:** newer model families and MCP server versions; all incidental. Swap in current model names/paths and everything runs. Dan future-proofs this explicitly ("tools will change and models will improve — we can't fixate").
**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("model names / local paths are period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.

# TAC-8 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

This is the final lesson; it compresses the whole course. Ordering rule: how much of *your practice* collapses if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is the spine — get these and you can rebuild the rest. Tier 2 is the machinery you actually operate. Tier 3 is the framing that keeps you allocating your time correctly after the course ends.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. Your codebase has two layers, and at least half your time goes to the second.**
The **application layer** is everything classical — app, database, infra, DevOps. The **agentic layer** is the ring wrapped around it: prompts, template meta prompts, and ADWs that operate the app for you. Tactic #8 is *Prioritize Agentics*: ≥50% of engineering time on the ring (more when bootstrapping).
*Say it Dan's way:* "As a good starting point… at least half your engineering time should be spent on the new agentic layer."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they nod at the ratio, then spend 100% of the week in the app layer "for the deadline" — and never build the layer that would have hit the next ten deadlines. The tactic is a **time-allocation change, not a belief.**

**2. One question compresses all eight tactics. Ask it daily.**
*"Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer?"* Every KPI, every leverage point, all eight tactics fold into this. There are exactly **three** acceptable reasons to answer "application layer": a deadline, testing something by hand, or running your prompts in-loop to verify they'll work out-loop. Anything else and "you're going sideways while other engineers move up."
*Say it Dan's way:* "Even if you forget all eight tactics, this is all you need to think about."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they answer it once, at course end, instead of "every day when you sit down to work."

**3. The smallest real agentic layer is three directories.**
The **Minimum Viable Agentic Layer**: `.claude/commands/` (prompts) + `specs/` (plans) + `adws/` (workflows). Not a framework, not a platform. The single rule: "you can compose code and reference other files and have this be isolated from your application layer." Scripting language is free choice (UV Python, Bun TS, shell).
*Why weak learners lose it:* they cargo-cult the *scaled* tree (hooks, triggers, state, worktrees, observability) on day one. Thin ring first; the scaled tree is where you END after value compounds.

**4. The most leveraged file isn't code — it's a prompt that writes prompts.**
A **template meta prompt** (like `chore.md`) generates a *plan* in a rigid format that encodes your engineering standards. The load-bearing section is the **Plan Format**: metadata, relevant files, **step-by-step tasks**, and **validation commands** — the plan ends by checking itself. `/implement` is a *higher-order prompt*: it takes that plan as its argument.
*Say it Dan's way:* "These are meta prompts… this is a prompt that generates a prompt."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they write prompts so specific they solve today's task once. Target the **problem class**, not the instance (nugget 10).

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. One script is categorically different from all your others: the gateway.**
`adw_prompt.py` doesn't compute a result — it hires an intelligence and files a report. It builds `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format stream-json --model … --dangerously-skip-permissions`, manages a unique `adw_id` and retries, and lands four files under `agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/`: the JSONL stream → JSON array → **final object** → your custom summary.
*Say it Dan's way:* "This script is the gateway into agentic coding… this ADW is calling an agent. This is distinctly different from any other type of code."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they skip the output tour. If you can't say what's in `cc_final_object.json` vs the summary, every later system (task boards, Notion factory, AEA) feels like magic instead of engineering.

**6. A composed ADW is two prompts and forty lines of glue — and the glue is where the guarantees live.**
`adw_chore_implement.py`: Phase 1 runs `/chore` as agent **planner**; the script **regex-extracts** the plan path from the agent's report; Phase 2 feeds that path to `/implement` as agent **builder**. It works ONLY because `/chore`'s Report section is a machine-parseable **contract** ("Return the path to the plan file created").
*Why weak learners lose it:* they think the halves are independent. Change `/chore`'s Report format and the regex breaks — deterministic code and non-deterministic prompt are **coupled by an explicit contract.**

**7. A multi-agent system can live in a single markdown file.**
app2's **Todone**: `tasks.md` + a 5-second cron loop runs seven agents in parallel. The state machine: `[]` → `[🟡, adw_id]` → `[✅ commit_hash, adw_id]` | `[❌, adw_id] // Failed: reason`; `[⏰]` is eligible only when every task above it is `✅` (a `❌` above blocks forever). Tags configure per task: `{opus}` upgrades the model, `{adw_plan_implement_update_task}` upgrades the workflow.
*Say it Dan's way:* "I'm not doing this, by the way."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they write one giant task and never touch tags or `⏰` — a to-do list with extra steps, not an orchestrator with dependencies, model routing, and workflow routing.

**8. Triggers are how you stay OUT of the loop.**
A trigger fires ADWs without you: a cron over `tasks.md`, a 15s Notion poller, a webhook, the AEA server. Map **PITER** onto any out-loop system: **P**rompt input (a Notion card), **T**rigger (the poll), **E**nvironment (`trees/` worktrees), **R**eview (board columns + live status). The claim trick that prevents double-pickup: flip status to *In progress* + `adw_id` the instant a task is grabbed.
*Why weak learners lose it:* they treat the Review column as bureaucracy. HIL Review + `continue - <prompt>` IS the steering loop — skip it and out-loop becomes fire-and-forget, i.e. fire-and-regret at scale.

**9. One agent, one prompt, one purpose — broken exactly once, on purpose.**
Focused agents mean focused, reproducible, testable context windows. The single sanctioned exception is app5's **AEA** (Agent Embedded Application): a product chat agent that persists `cc_session_id` in SQLite and passes it back with `--resume`, because conversation needs continuity across prompts, refreshes, and restarts. "Outside the loop is inside the application."
*Say it Dan's way:* "The power of agents isn't in one, it's in many."
*Why weak learners lose it:* two symmetric failures — treating the rule as optional (sprawling mega-agents you can't reproduce or test) OR treating it as absolute (refusing session continuity where the use case demands it).

**10. Solve problem classes, not one-off fixes.**
The unit of agentic-layer work is a *class* of problems. When one concise prompt produces an entire working MCP server, Dan declares the class closed.
*Say it Dan's way:* "I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV model context protocol servers. I've solved it. It's done."
*Test:* if your template can't absorb a request you didn't anticipate, you templated an **instance**, not a class.

**11. Always add feedback loops — that's what lets you drop the R.**
Every Plan Format ends in **validation commands**: the plan checks itself. Zero-touch engineering (ZTE) is when a dialed-in ADW is reliable enough that "the time you spend reviewing the work will be useless… you realize you're the bottleneck." Then **PITER → PITE**: drop the R.
*Say it Dan's way:* "You'll drop the R off… you will let your product ship itself."
*Why weak learners lose it:* they delete review before encoding it. The R is **replaced** by encoded feedback loops, never merely removed — PITE without validation is unsupervised risk.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you allocating correctly

**12. The app layer is a great place to start and a terrible place to stay.**
Building the agentic layer is **parabolic**: "put 10 minutes in, get two hours of value out or more." Deep application work feels productive, which is exactly the trap.
*Say it Dan's way:* "It's a great place to do deep work… It's a terrible place to stay. So many engineers are going to miss this mark."

**13. Don't think you're smarter than your own templated practices.**
Once your team's best engineering is encoded into a template meta prompt running in an ADW that kicks off five-to-ten agents per problem, you cannot out-execute it by hand.
*Say it Dan's way:* "Don't make the mistake of thinking you can outperform your team's best engineering practices encoded into a template metaprompt… your place of competition is now net-new innovation."
*Why weak learners lose it:* ego. They keep hand-fixing "just this one" and quietly opt out of the compounding system.

**14. Implementation is becoming a commodity; your value moved up the stack.**
"Not only is code a commodity, but the implementation as well." Value now lives in system design, domain encoding, quality control, and creative problem decomposition — "which you'll then encode in your ADWs." An agentic engineer "operates on living pieces of software that work while they sleep."

**15. This is a ring you thicken daily — you're orchestrating intelligence now.**
Picture the ring: thin at first, thicker every time you template a workflow, until machines that carry your judgment ship your way autonomously. That's the whole arc.
*Say it Dan's way:* "When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence."

---

6. Give the full `tasks.md` state machine including the blocking rule, and say what `{opus}` and `{adw_plan_implement_update_task}` each do.
7. State the one-agent rule, why it exists, and the single exception with its mechanism.
8. What has to be true before you convert PITER → PITE?
